title: Assured Equipment Grounding Conductor Program: Cord Checks and Tests
summary: If a site uses an assured equipment grounding conductor program instead of GFCIs, cords and tools must be inspected daily and tested on a schedule, and the results recorded.
talking_points: An assured equipment grounding conductor program (AEGCP) can be used in place of GFCIs for ground-fault protection. If your site uses one, these are the minimum rules.
A written description of the program must be kept at the jobsite, with the inspection and test procedures and schedule. It must be available to OSHA and to affected workers.
One or more competent persons run the program. They can spot hazards and are authorized to take prompt corrective action.
Visually inspect all cord sets, plugs, caps, receptacles, and cord-and-plug equipment before use each day. Look for deformed or missing pins and damaged insulation.
If you see damage outside or find it inside, take the equipment out of use until it is repaired.

Two tests are required on all equipment: a continuity test and a terminal connection test. Do them before first use, after repairs, after suspected damage, and every 3 months. Some exceptions are in 29 CFR 1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E)(4).

The continuity test shows the grounding conductor is electrically continuous. The terminal connection test shows it is connected to the right terminal at receptacles and plugs. A receptacle tester can do the second test on receptacles.
Keep a written record of the tests that shows which equipment passed and the last test date or test interval. It must be available to OSHA inspectors and affected workers.
site_hazards_to_check: Cords with missing or bent pins, cracked insulation, or damaged plugs
Damaged equipment still in use instead of out of service
Tools or cords with no test date or record
No written program or competent person on site
Tests overdue, such as after a repair or past 3 months
discussion_questions: Does our site use GFCIs or an assured grounding program, and where is the written program?
Who is the competent person who checks and tests our cords and tools?
How do we tag and remove a damaged cord from use?
